content: The Japanese Red Cross Society (JRCS) is the sole entity authorized by the government of Japan to collect donated blood. Each blood collection center under JRCS must obtain permission from the Minister of Health, Labour, and Welfare. The Ministry of Public Health provides accreditation for blood centers. Blood centers in various countries are certified under ISO 9001 and ISO 15189 standards, ensuring quality management and laboratory competence. In Malaysia, the Department of Standards oversees the certification of private healthcare facilities. Mauritius is certified under ISO 9001:2008 by the Mauritius Standards Bureau. In Mexico, the Mexican Accreditation Body (Entidad Mexicana de Acreditación) is responsible for certification. Blood centers are subject to annual inspections and audits by national authorities. For example, in New Zealand, blood services are accredited by MedSafe, the national medicines regulatory authority. In the United States, the haemovigilance system is voluntary, and some transfusion services are accredited by the Joint Commission or the AABB (American Association of Blood Banks). Educational programs for blood transfusion personnel are available in several countries, offering nationally recognized degrees or diplomas. These programs often include training in blood transfusion science and laboratory technology. National haemovigilance systems are in place in many countries to monitor donor-related and recipient-related adverse events. Regular inspections, licensing, and accreditation of blood transfusion services are conducted to ensure compliance with international standards. Countries like Sweden and Switzerland have comprehensive blood transfusion systems accredited under ISO standards. In Tunisia, the National Blood Transfusion Centre is certified under ISO 9001 since 2004, with annual renewal audits. The Pacific Paramedical Training Centre (PPTC) offers a two-year distance learning course in medical laboratory technology, including blood transfusion science. Any new transfusion structure must receive prior authorization from the Ministry of Health through the National Blood Transfusion Centre. In Serbia, laboratories under the Blood Transfusion Institute of Serbia (BTIS) are accredited under SRPS ISO/IEC 17025 and the European Federation of Immunogenetics (EFI). Similarly, South Africa's blood services are accredited by SANAS (South African National Accreditation System). International organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the Global Fund, and the American Red Cross provide support for blood transfusion services in various countries. For example, the WHO collaborates with countries like Cambodia, Cameroon, and Ethiopia to strengthen their blood transfusion systems. In summary, blood transfusion services worldwide are regulated and accredited by national and international bodies to ensure safety, quality, and compliance with global standards.
